### The framing problem for tonight

> **Where should Washington, Oregon, and Idaho add their next 10 PM2.5 monitors?**
> The regulatory PM2.5 network is built for compliance. It's dense around
> Seattle, Portland, and Boise and thin almost everywhere else. In 2024 EPA
> tightened the annual PM2.5 standard to 9.0 µg/m³, so the gaps now matter:
> some unmonitored valleys could be over the new standard without anyone
> knowing. You'll pull every monitor's current **annual PM2.5 design value**
> straight from EPA's public ArcGIS feature service. Covariates come from
> USGS and Census services: elevation, population density, and distance to
> the nearest major road. You'll fit a model and rank the unmonitored
> locations most likely to have high annual PM2.5.

Nothing here is new spatial theory: you've done spatial joins (Module 4),
raster/vector integration (Modules 5–6 and 8), and mapping (Module 7). Module 9
adds three pieces to the pipeline. A *statistical model* becomes the
"integrate" stage. A *language bridge* means you aren't stuck with whatever
library R or Python happens to have. And *live web services* replace the
downloaded file as your data source.

# Section 1 — The Bridge: How `reticulate` Actually Works {#sec-bridge}

*(Concept Input, ~10 min of tonight's live-coding segment)*

`reticulate` embeds a Python interpreter inside your R session. You aren't
switching between two programs — one process, two languages, objects passed
back and forth by name.

## 1a — Four ways to use Python from R

| Method | What it does | When you'd use it |
|---|---|---|
| `source_python("script.py")` | Runs a `.py` file, pulls its top-level functions/variables into R | You already have a Python module and just want to call its functions |
| `py_run_string("...")` | Runs a string of Python code in the shared session | A quick one-off Python snippet inside an R script |
| `repl_python()` | Drops you into an interactive Python prompt inside your R console; `exit` returns to R | Exploring interactively before you commit code to a chunk |
| Quarto `{python}` chunks (what this document uses) | Each chunk is Python, but shares the reticulate session with the R chunks around it | Writing a document where both languages appear as first-class code, not a side quest |

## 1b — Type conversion, the short version

| R | Python | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `data.frame` | `pandas.DataFrame` | Converts automatically, column types mostly preserved |
| `list` (named) | `dict` | Named list ↔ dict is the default two-way mapping |
| `list` (unnamed) | `list` | |
| numeric vector | NumPy array / list | Length-1 vectors become Python scalars |
| `NULL` | `None` | |
| `sf` object | *(no automatic conversion)* | Pass plain coordinates (lon/lat columns), WKT, or GeoJSON text instead. reticulate doesn't know GeoPandas' GeoDataFrame, so you're the bridge for spatial types (Section 2 passes lon/lat tables in both directions) |

## 1c — Live coding: pass an object each direction

```{r}
#| label: bridge-demo-r1

library(reticulate)

# An R data.frame — nothing python-flavored about it yet
monitor_counts_r <- data.frame(
  state = c("Washington", "Oregon", "Idaho"),
  n_monitors = c(30L, 25L, 12L)   # illustrative counts; Section 2 pulls the real ones
)
monitor_counts_r
```

```{python}
#| label: bridge-demo-py

# `r.monitor_counts_r` reaches back into the R chunk above — the data.frame
# arrives already converted to a pandas DataFrame, no export/import step.
import pandas as pd

monitor_counts_py = r.monitor_counts_r
monitor_counts_py["share"] = monitor_counts_py["n_monitors"] / monitor_counts_py["n_monitors"].sum()
monitor_counts_py
```

```{r}
#| label: bridge-demo-r2

# `py$monitor_counts_py` reaches forward into the Python chunk above —
# the pandas DataFrame arrives back as an R data.frame, edits and all.
monitor_counts_back <- py$monitor_counts_py
str(monitor_counts_back)
```

That round trip — R → Python → R, no files written, no kernel switched — is
the entire objective in miniature. Everything else this module does is that
same handoff applied to spatial data and a statistical model.

## 1d — When to reach for the bridge (and when not to)

| Reach for `reticulate` when… | Just pick one language when… |
|---|---|
| The library you need only exists in the other language (e.g. a specific `scikit-learn` estimator, or an R spatial-statistics package with no Python equivalent) | Both languages have a perfectly good option and switching buys you nothing |
| You want to compare two implementations of the same idea (tidymodels vs. scikit-learn) side by side in one document | The task is small enough that the bridge's overhead isn't worth explaining to whoever reads this next |
| You're prototyping in Python but the rest of your team's pipeline is R (or vice versa) | You're handing this off to someone who only knows one of the two languages — don't make them install both toolchains to read your code |

# Section 2 — Pulling Data From Web Services {#sec-webservices}

*(Concept Input, remainder of the live-coding segment)*

Module 9's objective names three request/response patterns. All three are
live services in this lab:

| Pattern | What you get back | What this lab pulls |
|---|---|---|
| **WMS** (Web Map Service) | A rendered image. You can look at it, but you can't query or join it | MRLC **NLCD 2021 land cover**, displayed for context only (Step 2e) |
| **WFS** (Web Feature Service) | Features: geometries plus attributes, through a standard OGC request | USGS **Watershed Boundary Dataset** HU6 basins, which serve as airsheds for spatial CV (Step 2b) |
| **REST API** (ArcGIS FeatureServer / MapServer / ImageServer) | Features, tables, or pixel values, filtered on the server with `where` and geometry parameters | EPA **PM2.5 annual design values** (2a); Census **TIGERweb** tracts and primary roads (2c); USGS **3DEP** elevation via `getSamples` (2d) |
| **Near-real-time feed** (IoT / SensorThings-style) | Time-stamped observations from physical devices, refreshed hourly or faster | EPA **AirNow** hourly monitor layer (Extended Application, Option 2) |

## 2a — Live services, with a safety net

Real endpoints go down, change schemas, and rate-limit — bad properties for a
notebook twenty people run at once. So every pull below does the same thing:
**try the live service first, save a cached copy, and fall back to that copy
if the service fails.** That's the production pattern too. Production
pipelines never assume an upstream service is up.

```{r}
#| label: setup-params

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(httr2)

study_states <- c("Washington", "Oregon", "Idaho")
study_fips   <- c("53", "41", "16")
study_bbox   <- st_bbox(c(xmin = -124.9, ymin = 41.9, xmax = -111.0, ymax = 49.1),
                        crs = st_crs(4326))

# CONUS Albers Equal Area (meters). Module 3's WA State Plane (EPSG:2926)
# doesn't cover a three-state study area, so we switch to a CRS that does.
target_crs <- 5070
grid_km    <- 50      # prediction grid cell size
min_gap_km <- 25      # a cell this close to an existing monitor counts as "monitored"

USE_CACHE  <- TRUE    # FALSE = live first, cache only as fallback; TRUE = read cache if present
cache_dir  <- "data/module9_cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
cache_gpkg <- file.path(cache_dir, "module9_cache.gpkg")

# Generic "live pull, or fall back to cache" wrapper for sf layers
pull_or_cache <- function(layer_name, pull_fn) {
  cached <- file.exists(cache_gpkg) && layer_name %in% st_layers(cache_gpkg)$name
  if (USE_CACHE && cached) return(st_read(cache_gpkg, layer = layer_name, quiet = TRUE))
  out <- tryCatch(pull_fn(), error = function(e) {
    message("Live pull for '", layer_name, "' failed: ", conditionMessage(e)); NULL
  })
  if (is.null(out) || nrow(out) == 0) {
    if (cached) {
      message("  -> using cached copy of '", layer_name, "'")
      return(st_read(cache_gpkg, layer = layer_name, quiet = TRUE))
    }
    stop("No live data and no cached copy for '", layer_name, "'.")
  }
  st_write(out, cache_gpkg, layer = layer_name, delete_layer = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
  out
}

# A ~20-line R version of what arcgislayers::arc_select() does for you:
# page through an ArcGIS REST /query endpoint, check exceededTransferLimit,
# bind the pages into one sf object. Used in Steps 2b and 2c.
arc_query_sf <- function(layer_url, ..., page_size = 2000, max_pages = 50) {
  pages <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(max_pages)) {
    txt <- request(paste0(layer_url, "/query")) |>
      req_url_query(..., outSR = 4326, f = "json",
                    resultOffset = (i - 1) * page_size,
                    resultRecordCount = page_size) |>
      req_timeout(180) |>
      req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_string()
    if (grepl('^\\s*\\{\\s*"error"', txt)) stop("ArcGIS error: ", substr(txt, 1, 300))
    pages[[i]] <- read_sf(txt, quiet = TRUE)              # GDAL's ESRIJSON driver
    if (!grepl('"exceededTransferLimit"\\s*:\\s*true', txt)) break
  }
  bind_rows(pages)
}
```

### Step 2a — The monitoring network: EPA PM2.5 design values (ArcGIS REST, Python)

EPA publishes design values for every criteria pollutant as a public ArcGIS
feature service. A **design value** is the statistic compared against the
standard; for annual PM2.5 it's a 3-year average of annual means. Layer `4`
is *PM2.5 Annual*. You query it the way ArcGIS Pro does behind the scenes:
an HTTP `GET` to `/query` with a `where` clause.

```{python}
#| label: pull-design-values

# [Python] Step 2a — query EPA's Air Quality Design Values FeatureServer
import os
import time
import json
import requests
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DV_LAYER = ("https://services.arcgis.com/cJ9YHowT8TU7DUyn/ArcGIS/rest/services/"
            "Air_Quality_Design_Values_for_Criteria_Pollutants/FeatureServer/4")

def arcgis_query(layer_url, where="1=1", out_fields="*", page_size=1000, **extra):
    """Page through an ArcGIS REST /query endpoint and return attribute dicts.

    This is what ArcGIS Pro, the ArcGIS API for Python, and R's arcgislayers
    all do under the hood: request a page, check exceededTransferLimit,
    request the next page."""
    rows, offset = [], 0
    while True:
        params = {"where": where, "outFields": out_fields, "returnGeometry": "false",
                  "resultOffset": offset, "resultRecordCount": page_size, "f": "json", **extra}
        resp = requests.get(f"{layer_url}/query", params=params, timeout=60)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        payload = resp.json()
        if "error" in payload:        # ArcGIS reports errors inside an HTTP 200 response
            raise RuntimeError(payload["error"])
        batch = payload.get("features", [])
        rows.extend(f["attributes"] for f in batch)
        if not batch or not payload.get("exceededTransferLimit"):
            break
        offset += len(batch)
    return rows

USE_CACHE = r.USE_CACHE
dv_cache = os.path.join(r.cache_dir, "pm25_design_values.csv")
where = "state_name IN ({})".format(",".join(f"'{s}'" for s in r.study_states))
fields = ("AQSID,local_site_name,state_name,county_name,latitude,longitude,"
          "dv_year,design_value,dv_validity_ind,edt_id")

try:
    if USE_CACHE and os.path.exists(dv_cache):
        raise RuntimeError("USE_CACHE is TRUE")
    dv_raw = pd.DataFrame(arcgis_query(DV_LAYER, where=where, out_fields=fields))
    dv_raw.to_csv(dv_cache, index=False)
    source = "live EPA FeatureServer"
except Exception as e:
    if USE_CACHE and os.path.exists(dv_cache):
        print("USE_CACHE = TRUE: reading the saved copy instead of calling the live service.")
    else:
        print("Live pull failed (", e, "); falling back to the saved copy.")
    dv_raw = pd.read_csv(dv_cache)
    source = "cached copy"

print(f"{len(dv_raw)} design-value rows from {source}")
dv_raw.head()
```

The raw table can hold more than one row per site: several design-value
periods, and sometimes a separate row with exceptional events (wildfire
smoke, for example) excluded. Before modeling, reduce it to **one row per
monitor for the latest period**:

```{python}
#| label: clean-design-values

dv = dv_raw.copy()
dv["dv_year"] = pd.to_datetime(dv["dv_year"], unit="ms").dt.year   # ArcGIS dates are epoch milliseconds
latest = int(dv["dv_year"].max())
dv = dv[(dv["dv_year"] == latest) & dv["design_value"].notna()]

valid = dv["dv_validity_ind"].astype(str).str.upper().str.startswith("Y")
if valid.any():
    dv = dv[valid]
else:
    print("Note: no rows flagged valid; check dv_validity_ind values:",
          dv_raw["dv_validity_ind"].unique())

print("Exceptional-event variants present:", dict(dv["edt_id"].value_counts()))
dv = dv.sort_values("edt_id").drop_duplicates("AQSID")    # one consistent row per site

monitors_df = (dv.rename(columns={"longitude": "lon", "latitude": "lat",
                                  "design_value": "pm25_dv"})
                 [["AQSID", "local_site_name", "state_name", "lon", "lat", "pm25_dv"]]
                 .reset_index(drop=True))

print(f"{len(monitors_df)} monitors with a valid {latest - 2}–{latest} annual PM2.5 design value")
print(f"{(monitors_df.pm25_dv > 9.0).sum()} are above the 2024 NAAQS of 9.0 µg/m³")
monitors_df.describe()
```

### Step 2b — Airsheds from a WFS: USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset (R)

Air pollution pools in basins. Think of Willamette Valley inversions or
woodsmoke in the Boise valley. Hydrologic basins (HU6) are a decent stand-in
for airsheds, and Step 2 of the lab uses them to build honest
cross-validation folds. USGS serves the WBD as an OGC **WFS**.

GDAL, and therefore `sf` and GeoPandas, speaks WFS natively, but only part of
that works against this server:

| Request | Through GDAL (`st_layers()` / `st_read()`) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `GetCapabilities` (list the layers) | `st_layers("WFS:...")` | Works |
| `GetFeature`, no filter | `st_read("WFS:...", layer = ...)` | Works, but downloads every HU6 basin in the country, as curved `MultiSurface` geometries that break `st_intersects()` and `st_cast()` |
| `GetFeature` with a bbox | `st_read(..., wkt_filter = ...)` or GeoPandas `bbox=` | **HTTP 403**, whichever WFS version you force |

GDAL builds its own filtered `GetFeature` request, and this ArcGIS-hosted
WFS rejects it. A hand-written WFS 2.0 request with the same bbox works. So
the code below uses GDAL for `GetCapabilities` and writes the `GetFeature`
URL itself. That's a lesson in its own right: standards compliance varies by
server, and sometimes you have to drop down a level to the raw request.

```{r}
#| label: pull-basins-wfs

# [R] Step 2b — HU6 basins from the USGS WBD WFS (REST fallback if WFS is down)
wbd_wfs  <- "https://hydro-wfs.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/services/wbd/MapServer/WFSServer"
wbd_rest <- "https://hydro.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/wbd/MapServer/3"   # 6-digit HU

basins <- pull_or_cache("wbd_hu6", function() {
  out <- tryCatch({
    # GetCapabilities through GDAL: this part works
    lyrs <- st_layers(paste0("WFS:", wbd_wfs))$name
    message("WFS layers on offer: ", paste(lyrs, collapse = ", "))
    hu6  <- grep("Basin", lyrs, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)[1]   # HU6 = "Basin"
    if (is.na(hu6)) stop("couldn't find the HU6 (Basin) layer in GetCapabilities")

    # GetFeature by hand: GDAL's own bbox request gets HTTP 403 from this server.
    # WFS 2.0 + EPSG:4326 means lat/lon axis order: ymin,xmin,ymax,xmax
    bbox_latlon <- paste(c(study_bbox[["ymin"]], study_bbox[["xmin"]],
                           study_bbox[["ymax"]], study_bbox[["xmax"]]), collapse = ",")
    gml <- tempfile(fileext = ".gml")
    request(wbd_wfs) |>
      req_url_query(service = "WFS", version = "2.0.0", request = "GetFeature",
                    typeNames = hu6, count = 500,
                    bbox = paste0(bbox_latlon, ",urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326")) |>
      req_timeout(180) |>
      req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
      req_perform(path = gml)

    # type = 6 forces MULTIPOLYGON, linearizing any curved MultiSurface geometry
    st_read(gml, type = 6, quiet = TRUE) |> st_make_valid()
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("WFS failed (", conditionMessage(e), "); trying the WBD REST endpoint")
    arc_query_sf(wbd_rest, where = "1=1", outFields = "huc6,name",
                 geometry = paste(study_bbox, collapse = ","),
                 geometryType = "esriGeometryEnvelope", inSR = 4326,
                 spatialRel = "esriSpatialRelIntersects", maxAllowableOffset = 0.01)
  })
  # WFS and REST spell field names differently (HUC6 vs huc6): lowercase the
  # attribute names, but leave the geometry column's name alone
  geom_col <- attr(out, "sf_column")
  nm <- names(out)
  nm[nm != geom_col] <- tolower(nm[nm != geom_col])
  names(out) <- nm
  select(out, any_of(c("huc6", "name")))
})

cat(nrow(basins), "HU6 basins intersect the study area\n")
```

The REST fallback isn't just a backup. The same USGS basins are also
published as an ArcGIS REST layer, which filters on the server with no
axis-order or geometry-type surprises. When a provider offers both, the REST
route is usually the simpler one. WFS is still worth knowing, because many
agencies publish *only* OGC services. Its successor, OGC API – Features,
uses plain URLs and GeoJSON and avoids most of these quirks.

### Step 2c — Population density and roads from Census TIGERweb (ArcGIS REST, R)

TIGERweb is the Census Bureau's ArcGIS Server. Its tract layer carries the
2020 census population (`POP100`) and land area (`AREALAND`), which gives
you population density. Its *Primary Roads* layer gives you interstates and
limited-access highways, which gives you distance-to-road. Both go through
`arc_query_sf()`, the small paging helper defined in the setup chunk above.

```{r}
#| label: pull-tracts-roads

tiger <- "https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/TIGERweb"

tracts <- pull_or_cache("tiger_tracts", function() {
  arc_query_sf(paste0(tiger, "/Tracts_Blocks/MapServer/10"),
               where = sprintf("STATE IN (%s)", paste0("'", study_fips, "'", collapse = ",")),
               outFields = "GEOID,STATE,POP100,AREALAND",
               maxAllowableOffset = 0.005,        # generalize on the server: ~500 m
               page_size = 4000)
})
stopifnot("POP100" %in% names(tracts))            # schema check — services do change

roads <- pull_or_cache("tiger_primary_roads", function() {
  arc_query_sf(paste0(tiger, "/Transportation_LargeScale/MapServer/0"),
               where = "1=1", outFields = "MTFCC",
               geometry = paste(study_bbox, collapse = ","),
               geometryType = "esriGeometryEnvelope", inSR = 4326,
               spatialRel = "esriSpatialRelIntersects",
               maxAllowableOffset = 0.002)
})

cat(nrow(tracts), "census tracts;", nrow(roads), "primary-road segments\n")
```

Now build the **prediction grid**: 50 km cells covering the three states,
each with a population density (from the tract under its center) and a
distance to the nearest primary road.

```{r}
#| label: build-grid

tracts_p <- tracts |>
  st_transform(target_crs) |>
  mutate(pop_density = as.numeric(POP100) / pmax(as.numeric(AREALAND) / 1e6, 0.01)) |>  # people / km²
  select(pop_density)

roads_p <- st_transform(roads, target_crs)

grid_geom <- st_make_grid(tracts_p, cellsize = grid_km * 1000, what = "polygons")
grid      <- st_sf(cell_id = seq_along(grid_geom), geometry = grid_geom)

grid_ctr <- grid |>
  st_centroid() |>
  st_join(tracts_p, join = st_intersects, left = FALSE) |>   # drops cells outside WA/OR/ID
  distinct(cell_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

nearest <- st_nearest_feature(grid_ctr, roads_p)
grid_ctr$dist_road_km <- as.numeric(st_distance(grid_ctr, roads_p[nearest, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 1000

grid <- grid |> filter(cell_id %in% grid_ctr$cell_id)

# Hand the cell centers to Python as plain lon/lat — sf doesn't cross the bridge
grid_ll    <- st_coordinates(st_transform(grid_ctr, 4326))
grid_pts_r <- data.frame(cell_id = grid_ctr$cell_id, lon = grid_ll[, 1], lat = grid_ll[, 2])

cat(nrow(grid), "grid cells inside the study area\n")
```

### Step 2d — Elevation from the 3DEP ImageServer (ArcGIS REST, Python)

An ImageServer serves pixels, not features. Its `getSamples` operation
returns the raster value at a set of points you send it, so you never
download a DEM. This step samples the monitors from Step 2a *and* the grid
cells that R just built, and the grid arrives here as `r.grid_pts_r`.

```{python}
#| label: pull-elevation

# [Python] Step 2d — sample USGS 3DEP elevation at monitors + grid cell centers
ELEV = ("https://elevation.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/"
        "3DEPElevation/ImageServer/getSamples")

def sample_3dep(lon, lat, chunk=25, tries=5):
    """Return elevation (m) at each lon/lat via 3DEP getSamples, in input order."""
    lon, lat = np.asarray(lon, float), np.asarray(lat, float)
    out = np.full(len(lon), np.nan)
    for start in range(0, len(lon), chunk):
        pts = [[x, y] for x, y in zip(lon[start:start + chunk], lat[start:start + chunk])]
        for attempt in range(tries):                  # the service intermittently returns 502/504
            resp = requests.post(ELEV, data={
                "geometry": json.dumps({"points": pts, "spatialReference": {"wkid": 4326}}),
                "geometryType": "esriGeometryMultipoint",
                "returnFirstValueOnly": "true",
                "f": "json"}, timeout=120)
            if resp.status_code < 500:
                break
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        samples = resp.json().get("samples", [])
        ids = [s["locationId"] for s in samples]
        base = 0 if 0 in ids else 1                   # locationId is 0- or 1-based depending on server
        for s in samples:
            try:
                out[start + s["locationId"] - base] = float(s["value"])
            except (ValueError, TypeError, IndexError):
                pass                                  # "NoData" stays NaN
    return out

grid_pts = r.grid_pts_r
elev_cache = os.path.join(r.cache_dir, f"elevation_{int(r.grid_km)}km.csv")
try:
    if USE_CACHE and os.path.exists(elev_cache):
        raise RuntimeError("USE_CACHE is TRUE")
    monitors_df["elevation_m"] = sample_3dep(monitors_df.lon, monitors_df.lat)
    grid_pts["elevation_m"]    = sample_3dep(grid_pts.lon, grid_pts.lat)
    pd.concat([
        monitors_df.assign(kind="monitor", key=monitors_df.AQSID.astype(str))[["kind", "key", "elevation_m"]],
        grid_pts.assign(kind="grid", key=grid_pts.cell_id.astype(int).astype(str))[["kind", "key", "elevation_m"]],
    ]).to_csv(elev_cache, index=False)
except Exception as e:
    if USE_CACHE and os.path.exists(elev_cache):
        print("USE_CACHE = TRUE: reading saved elevations instead of calling the live service.")
    else:
        print("Live elevation pull failed (", e, "); falling back to the saved copy.")
    cache = pd.read_csv(elev_cache, dtype={"key": str})
    look = dict(zip(cache.kind + ":" + cache.key, cache.elevation_m))
    monitors_df["elevation_m"] = pd.to_numeric(
        [look.get(f"monitor:{k}") for k in monitors_df.AQSID.astype(str)], errors="coerce")
    grid_pts["elevation_m"] = pd.to_numeric(
        [look.get(f"grid:{int(k)}") for k in grid_pts.cell_id], errors="coerce")

print("Monitors missing elevation:", int(monitors_df.elevation_m.isna().sum()))
print("Grid cells missing elevation:", int(grid_pts.elevation_m.isna().sum()))
```

### Step 2e — The WMS contrast: NLCD land cover as a picture (R)

You can **see** land cover through MRLC's WMS. Try getting a number out of
it. Every request returns PNG tiles, which are pixels colored for display.
To *model* with NLCD you'd need a WCS or ImageServer, a Cloud-Optimized
GeoTIFF (Module 10), or a download. That's the WMS trap from tonight's slides.

```{r}
#| label: wms-view

library(leaflet)

mon <- py$monitors_df

leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") |>
  addWMSTiles(
    "https://www.mrlc.gov/geoserver/mrlc_display/NLCD_2021_Land_Cover_L48/wms",
    layers  = "NLCD_2021_Land_Cover_L48",
    options = WMSTileOptions(format = "image/png", transparent = TRUE, opacity = 0.55),
    attribution = "MRLC NLCD 2021 (WMS)"
  ) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = mon, lng = ~lon, lat = ~lat, radius = 5,
                   color = "#4b2e83", fillOpacity = 0.9, stroke = FALSE,
                   label = ~sprintf("%s: %.1f µg/m³", local_site_name, pm25_dv)) |>
  fitBounds(-124.9, 41.9, -111.0, 49.1)
# If the land-cover tiles come back blank, MRLC has renamed the layer: open
# .../wms?service=WMS&request=GetCapabilities and copy the layer's <Name>.
```

## 2f — SensorThings and the IoT piece of the objective

Design values are a slow-moving, 3-year statistic. That's exactly why they
work as a modeling target. A real-time platform answers a different
question, such as *"what is PM2.5 at this monitor right now, and over the
last 24 hours?"* OGC's **SensorThings API** (named in this module's required
reading) standardizes that. Each device is a `Thing` with `Datastreams` of
time-stamped `Observations`. EPA's **AirNow** hourly feature layer is the
same idea published as an ArcGIS layer, and Extended Application Option 2
uses it. Learn the vocabulary (`Thing`, `Datastream`, `Observation`). The
modeling in this lab sticks to the stable annual statistic on purpose.

# Section 3 — Guided Lab: Build the PM2.5 Gap Model {#sec-lab}

*(Guided Lab, ~50–60 min)*

**Goal:** a `predict_exposure()` pipeline that takes the monitors and
covariates from Section 2, fits a spatial model, and ranks the unmonitored
grid cells with the highest predicted annual PM2.5. That ranking is the
shortlist for the next 10 monitors.

## Step 1 — Spatial join: attach covariates to each monitor

```{r}
#| label: lab-step1

# [R] Step 1 — monitors (from Python) + tract density + road distance + basin
monitors_sf <- st_as_sf(py$monitors_df, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(target_crs) |>                        # match the covariates' CRS before joining
  st_join(tracts_p, join = st_intersects) |>
  distinct(AQSID, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  st_join(st_transform(basins, target_crs) |> select(huc6), join = st_intersects) |>
  distinct(AQSID, .keep_all = TRUE)

nearest_m <- st_nearest_feature(monitors_sf, roads_p)
monitors_sf$dist_road_km <- as.numeric(
  st_distance(monitors_sf, roads_p[nearest_m, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 1000

monitors_sf <- monitors_sf |>
  mutate(log_pop_density = log10(pop_density + 1),
         huc6 = coalesce(as.character(huc6), "unknown"))

cat("Monitors with a complete covariate set:",
    sum(complete.cases(st_drop_geometry(monitors_sf)[, c("pm25_dv", "log_pop_density",
                                                          "dist_road_km", "elevation_m")])),
    "of", nrow(monitors_sf), "\n")
head(st_drop_geometry(monitors_sf))

# Save the modeling table (complete rows, no basin column) for the
# slide demos: Concept slides "Preparing Data" → "reticulate in Action" → "Fit → Predict"
monitors_sf |>
  select(AQSID, local_site_name, pm25_dv, log_pop_density, dist_road_km, elevation_m) |>
  filter(!is.na(pm25_dv), !is.na(log_pop_density), !is.na(dist_road_km), !is.na(elevation_m)) |>
  st_write(file.path(cache_dir, "monitors_covariates.gpkg"), delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
```

## Step 2 — The naive-split trap (why this isn't just `train_test_split()`)

Before fitting anything, notice that the monitors aren't independent
observations. Three Portland-area monitors breathe the same air (Tobler's
First Law again). Split them randomly and a test monitor usually has a
training neighbor a few kilometers away. The model then "passes" by
memorizing the neighbor instead of learning how population, roads, and
terrain relate to PM2.5. Watch it happen:

```{r}
#| label: lab-step2-naive

# [R] Step 2a — naive random cross-validation (the wrong way, done on purpose)
library(tidymodels)

monitors_cv <- monitors_sf |>
  filter(!is.na(pm25_dv), !is.na(log_pop_density), !is.na(dist_road_km), !is.na(elevation_m))

model_data <- monitors_cv |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(pm25_dv, log_pop_density, dist_road_km, elevation_m)

set.seed(9)
naive_folds <- vfold_cv(model_data, v = 5)

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("regression")

rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(rf_spec) |>
  add_formula(pm25_dv ~ log_pop_density + dist_road_km + elevation_m)

naive_results <- fit_resamples(rf_wf, resamples = naive_folds,
                               metrics = metric_set(rmse))
naive_rmse <- collect_metrics(naive_results) |> filter(.metric == "rmse") |> pull(mean)
cat("Naive random 5-fold CV RMSE:", round(naive_rmse, 2), "µg/m³\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: lab-step2-spatial

# [R] Step 2b — spatial block cross-validation (the fix)
library(spatialsample)

set.seed(9)
spatial_folds <- spatial_block_cv(monitors_cv, v = 5)

spatial_results <- fit_resamples(rf_wf, resamples = spatial_folds,
                                 metrics = metric_set(rmse))
spatial_rmse <- collect_metrics(spatial_results) |> filter(.metric == "rmse") |> pull(mean)
cat("Spatial block 5-fold CV RMSE:", round(spatial_rmse, 2), "µg/m³\n")

cat("\nGap:", round(spatial_rmse - naive_rmse, 2),
    "µg/m³ higher error once nearby monitors can't leak into each other's fold.\n")
cat("That gap is the honest number: it's what you'd actually see predicting\n")
cat("an unmonitored valley, which is the whole point of this exercise.\n")
```

With a few dozen real monitors the exact numbers will move with the seed,
and with whatever EPA published most recently. The required `tidymodels`
reading (geocompx's spatial-ML post) shows the same naive-vs-spatial gap on
a larger dataset (0.94 → 1.41 RMSE) if you want a more stable reference.
Take away the *direction* of the gap, not its size. Spatial CV reports the
more honest number, and it's usually worse.

## Step 3 — Fit the model both ways: tidymodels *and* scikit-learn

This is where the language bridge earns its keep. Fit the same random forest
in R (`tidymodels`/`ranger`) and in Python (`scikit-learn`). Python gets a
second kind of spatial CV: **grouping by HU6 basin**, the WFS layer from
Step 2b. A whole airshed is held out at a time.

```{r}
#| label: lab-step3-r

# [R] Step 3a — final tidymodels fit on all monitors
final_rf_fit <- rf_wf |> fit(data = model_data)
final_rf_fit

# Hand Python the same rows, plus the basin ID to group on
model_data_py <- monitors_cv |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(pm25_dv, log_pop_density, dist_road_km, elevation_m, huc6)
```

```{python}
#| label: lab-step3-py

# [Python] Step 3b — scikit-learn, with the data handed across the bridge
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, GroupKFold, cross_val_score

md = r.model_data_py
feats = ["log_pop_density", "dist_road_km", "elevation_m"]
X, y, groups = md[feats], md["pm25_dv"], md["huc6"]

rf_sklearn = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=9)

naive_cv = -cross_val_score(rf_sklearn, X, y, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                            cv=KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=9)).mean()

k = min(5, groups.nunique())                      # can't have more folds than basins
basin_cv = -cross_val_score(rf_sklearn, X, y, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                            cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=k), groups=groups).mean()

rf_sklearn.fit(X, y)
print(f"scikit-learn RF on {len(X)} monitors across {groups.nunique()} HU6 basins")
print(f"  naive KFold RMSE:              {naive_cv:.2f} µg/m³")
print(f"  basin-grouped GroupKFold RMSE: {basin_cv:.2f} µg/m³")
print("Feature importances:", dict(zip(feats, rf_sklearn.feature_importances_.round(3))))
```

Two implementations, one dataset, one document, and no exported CSVs or
numbers copied between notebooks. Objectives 1 and 2 are both covered by
these chunks.

## Step 4 — Predict across the grid and rank the shortlist

```{r}
#| label: lab-step4

# [R] Step 4 — predict every grid cell, then rank the ones far from any monitor
grid_cov <- grid_ctr |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(py$grid_pts[, c("cell_id", "elevation_m")], by = "cell_id") |>
  mutate(log_pop_density = log10(pop_density + 1)) |>
  filter(!is.na(elevation_m), !is.na(dist_road_km), !is.na(log_pop_density))

grid_cov$pred_pm25 <- predict(final_rf_fit, new_data = grid_cov)$.pred

predicted <- grid |> inner_join(grid_cov, by = "cell_id")

# "Unmonitored" = cell center more than min_gap_km from every existing monitor
gap_m <- apply(st_distance(st_centroid(predicted), monitors_sf), 1, min)
predicted$nearest_monitor_km <- as.numeric(gap_m) / 1000

candidates <- predicted |>
  filter(nearest_monitor_km > min_gap_km) |>
  arrange(desc(pred_pm25))

shortlist <- candidates |> slice_head(n = 10)

cat("Top 10 candidate cells for new PM2.5 monitors:\n")
print(st_drop_geometry(shortlist) |>
        transmute(cell_id, pred_pm25 = round(pred_pm25, 1),
                  nearest_monitor_km = round(nearest_monitor_km),
                  over_naaqs = pred_pm25 > 9.0))
```

## Step 5 — Map it

```{r}
#| label: lab-step5

# [R] Step 5 — predicted surface + basins + existing monitors + shortlist
library(tmap)
tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(predicted) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "pred_pm25",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted annual\nPM2.5 (µg/m³)")) +
  tm_shape(st_transform(basins, target_crs)) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(monitors_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "black", size = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(st_centroid(shortlist)) +
  tm_dots(fill = "#00bcd4", size = 0.6) +
  tm_title("Predicted annual PM2.5: existing monitors (black) vs. shortlist (cyan)")
```

# 🔍 Module 9 — Self-Check Questions

Work through these without looking at the chunks above, then verify.

**The bridge**

1. Name the four ways to run Python from R that Section 1 covers. Which one does this document use, and why does that mean you never had to switch a kernel?
2. Inside a Python chunk, how do you reach an object created in the R chunk above it? How does it work in reverse?
3. `sf` objects don't convert automatically across the bridge. What did Steps 2c and 2d pass across instead, and in which direction?

**Web services**

4. What's the practical difference between what the NLCD WMS returned in Step 2e and what the WBD WFS returned in Step 2b? Which one could you feed into a spatial join? And why did Step 2b write its own `GetFeature` request instead of letting `st_read()` do it?
5. Steps 2a, 2c, and 2d all hit ArcGIS REST endpoints, but three different kinds (FeatureServer, MapServer, ImageServer). What did you get back from each, and which operation did you call?
6. What does `exceededTransferLimit` tell you, and what would happen to your monitor count if your code ignored it?

**Modeling and the naive-split trap**

7. Why did the naive 5-fold CV in Step 2a report a *better* (lower) RMSE than spatial block CV in Step 2b? Which number would hold up for an unmonitored valley?
8. What do `spatial_block_cv()` (R) and `GroupKFold` grouped by HU6 basin (Python) both guarantee that plain `vfold_cv()` / `KFold` don't? Why are basins a reasonable grouping for *air* pollution?

**Putting it together**

9. Step 4 excludes cells within `min_gap_km` of an existing monitor before ranking. What would the top 10 look like without that filter, and why would that list be useless to a monitoring program?
10. Name one thing in Section 2 that can break with live services that never broke with synthetic data, and say how this lab handles it.
